newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bildt says Bosnia peace hinges on NATO presence.
newsitem.headline: Bildt says Bosnia peace hinges on NATO presence.

text.p: International envoy Carl Bildt warned on Friday that Bosnia's fragile peace could collapse if NATO peacekeeping troops withdraw in a year when their current mandate expires.
"If we were to walk away from the entire thing tomorrow, I think it is likely to fall apart," Bildt, who is due to step down this month as High Representative to Bosnia, told reporters.

The 31,000-strong NATO-led peace force is due to withdraw in June 1998, but Bildt said it was vital the alliance commit to staying in Bosnia to discourage political leaders from contemplating a return to war.
"I do not see a massive troop presence for the long term future nor do I see a need for it," Bildt said.

"But there needs to be a deterrent function, so that when we say we are not going to tolerate a resumption of hostilities, people know that these are words that can be backed up and can be backed up with force."

Bildt, who served 18 months overseeing the civilian side of the Dayton peace accords, said he regretted the international community's willingness to allow indicted war criminals to remain at large, undermining peace efforts.
"No government has ever been willing to give me the means to do anything on the war crimes issue," he said.

Linking economic aid to cooperation with the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague would never succeed in forcing the extradition of suspects such as former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, Bildt said.
"These are far too significant issues for the political leaderships to give in because of money," he said.
Bildt said he welcomed tough talk from U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on the issue and hinted that Western governments may be forced to arrest indicted war criminals sooner or later.
"We will see. The instruments are there," he said.
Arresting suspects would only represent a first step in coming to terms with war crimes committed during the 1992-95 conflict, he said.
"The key thing will of course be the trials, and the verdicts, and the aftermath of the verdicts. That's a long process which will have a profound impact on the political environment here," he said.
NATO has so far ruled out "manhunts" for indicted war criminals, fearing such arrests could cause a backlash against its troops and disrupt relations with rival armies.
Bildt said he welcomed a strongly-worded declaration on Bosnia issued by major powers at a summit last week in Sintra, Portugal.

The former Swedish prime minister said the first test of the warning from Sintra would come next month, when former warring factions must start rebuilding an integrated telephone network by a July 15 deadline.

The country's Moslem-Croat federation has so far refused to agree to a European Union proposal to build a new telephone system. They say the EU project would further divide the country by creating a largely separate telephone network in Serb-controlled territory.
The United States and European powers in the peace implementation council have threatened unspecified penalties if one of the Bosnian factions does not "cooperate fully" with the telephone project.
